title: Abu Talib dies
hook: the uncle who protected him dies in the same year, and the shield is gone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadijah dies. Your line was: he never forgot her. Whose story did you tell, or whose friend did you do something for? Day seven hundred forty-nine.

Dust, thrown from the street onto his head, as he walks home through Mecca. Just dust. A small, humiliating thing. He goes home with it still in his hair, and his daughter gets up to wash it off, and she's crying as she does it. He says to her, don't cry, my daughter, Allah will protect your father. Ibn Ishaq tells this scene, and he adds why it could happen now, when it couldn't before: the man who had kept the street from touching him was gone. Today: Abu Talib.
screen: `DUST ON HIS HEAD.` → `HIS DAUGHTER WEEPS.` → `WHY NOW?`

segments.voice: Abu Talib was his uncle, the one who took him in as a boy and, as the sirah tells it, refused again and again to hand him over when the leaders of Quraysh came asking. He led the clan into the valley during the boycott rather than give him up. He was the shield. Then, in the same year as Khadijah, Ibn Ishaq says, he is dying. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene at his bedside. The Prophet comes in and finds two leaders of Quraysh already there, Abu Jahl among them. He says to his uncle: say there is no god but Allah, a word I can plead for you with before Allah. The two men answer at once: will you leave the religion of Abd al-Muttalib? In Bukhari's report his last words hold to the religion of Abd al-Muttalib, his father. The Prophet says he will keep asking forgiveness for him unless he's forbidden. Muslims read this scene in different ways. In the Sunni hadith collections, it stands as the account of his death, and the report itself links it to two verses, one of them in surah twenty-eight, saying that the Prophet does not guide whom he loves; Allah guides whom He wills. Shia Muslims hold that Abu Talib was a believer who kept his faith quiet to keep his protection strong, and they honor him as such. Both remember the same thing about his life: he protected his nephew when it cost him. And then the protection was gone. The dust in the street is how the sirah shows it. That is what a shield is. Often nobody sees it until it isn't there. And this week has been full of shields: a just king across the sea, Meccans of conscience, a wife who held him up. Today, at home in Mecca, the shield of his own clan falls.
screen: `THE UNCLE WHO WOULDN'T HAND HIM OVER.` · `SAY THE WORD, UNCLE.` · `SUNNI AND SHIA READINGS.` · `A SHIELD IS SEEN WHEN IT'S GONE.` · then, large: `THE SHIELD IS GONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a protector while you can. Settle and breathe. Think back over your life for the people who stood between you and something hard. A parent, an older sibling, a teacher who covered for you, a friend who said no, leave them alone. Some of them never told you. Pick one who is still living. Let yourself see what they actually did, and what it might have cost them. Then decide how you'll thank them: a message, a call, a sentence the next time you see them. Muslims often ask Allah to reward such a person; if you pray, you can too. The bell holds the time.
Abu Talib. The uncle who protected him through the boycott dies, and the street can reach him now that the shield is gone. Today's word.
Your line: the shield is gone. Today, send the thanks you planned to one person who protected you, before another day passes. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims learn Abu Talib's protection and death as part of the Meccan sirah; Sunni and Shia Muslims understand his faith differently, and Shia Muslims honor him as a believer.
